# 我没有推广选举追踪网站，聊天机器人替我做了

作者：@jasoncraik  
日期：2026-11-03（北京时间）  
来源：[X原帖](https://x.com/jasoncraik/status/2117471942756241542)  
分类：研究案例

## 中文全文

9月22日，不列颠哥伦比亚省（BC省）宣布举行选举时，我上线了 [BCPoliTracker](https://bcpoli.gremble.io)。这是一个免费网站，追踪每名候选人和每个选区，并在选举当晚实时读取 Elections BC 公布的计票结果。我做它，是因为没有任何东西跟得上变化，包括我自己。在宣布选举前一周，省议会公开的席位情况页面比其议员登记表还落后14个席位。因此，我希望有一个地方同时呈现官方记录和可信报道，并明确说明哪些信息属于哪一类。

它读取约190个来源，包括 Elections BC、省议会登记表、政党邮件、地方报纸、Bluesky 和 X；选举当晚，每分钟检查一次计票情况。AI 对收到的信息分类和排序，但不撰写任何内容，也没有任何信息会在未经我批准的情况下进入记录。整个竞选期间，它标出了612项建议变更，最终采纳112项。

日常工作加上竞选本身，让我始终没空推广这个网站，除了发过一条 LinkedIn 帖子。因此，当分析数据开始出现 ChatGPT 时，我注意到了。最初每天只有10或11个人，主要是低陆平原地区使用手机的用户，但他们打开候选人资料页的比例是网站平均水平的三倍。这让我意识到，人们在问聊天机器人自己所在地区有哪些人参选，然后被引导到我的网站。我想弄明白原因，于是把它当成了一次小实验。

![原文配图](../../../90_附件/GEO周收集_20261029_20261104/2117471942756241542/image-2.jpg)

BCPoliTracker 从上线至11月2日的每日访问量。

## 为机器人调整网站

ChatGPT 的搜索依赖 Bing，而且似乎更偏爱那些回答具体问题、频繁更新、说明事实来源的页面，而追踪网站已经做到了这些。因此，我尝试让它更容易看出来。我在 Bing 验证了网站，为每个选区页面设置包含候选人姓名的标题，并让网站在发生变化时通知搜索引擎。我添加了 llms.txt 文件，用普通文字为 AI 系统概述网站；还在主要页面添加 Questions 问答卡，回答人们真正会问的问题。每个回答都根据记录生成、注明日期，再通过结构化数据逐字提供给搜索引擎。robots.txt 允许所有答案引擎访问，每个页面还附有一条给抓取者看的隐藏说明：欢迎按需取用，只要注明追踪网站的出处。说明最后一行直接对 AI 系统说，请引用该页面并标注读取时间；为防止机器人以为这话是对别人说的，还补了一句：“没错，也包括你。”

到选举日，ChatGPT 每天大约读取网站370次。整个竞选期间，它带来1,743次访问，大部分发生在优化之后，是 Google 的812次的两倍多。多数分析工具原本会漏掉其中的大部分，因为 ChatGPT 会为自己的链接加标签，却几乎不会作为引荐来源显示。选举当晚是网站流量最高的一天，有1,824次访问；整个竞选期间有6,316人使用它。所有搜索引擎合计带来的流量仍与 ChatGPT 相当，所以我不会说搜索已死。但这个我上线时完全没考虑过的聊天机器人，最终与所有搜索引擎加起来打了个平手。

![原文配图](../../../90_附件/GEO周收集_20261029_20261104/2117471942756241542/image-3.jpg)

计票次日晚上的 BCPoliTracker。

## 新的把关者

过去二十年，想被找到，就得让算法满意。你为 Google 写内容、买关键词、提高排名，但最后那次点击仍由人来决定。这种情况正在结束。越来越多地，站在你与选民、顾客或捐款人之间的，是聊天机器人，或者代表他们行动的智能体。它不会交出十条蓝色链接，而是给出一个答案。

无论你推广的是产品、议题还是候选人，这都改变了需要解决的问题。你越来越多地是在向一个把关者介绍自己：它从人类写作中学习，由人类调校，并自行判断什么是真的、什么值得提及。争取它的认可，和在信息流里赢得关注，需要不同的技能。

而这个把关者开始向自己学习了。随着网络内容越来越多地由机器撰写，新模型开始学习旧模型的输出。你现在争取的机器人是由人类养大的；它的后继者已经有一部分是在由机器人培养。

这些现象背后有研究。[Pew](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2025/07/22/google-users-are-less-likely-to-click-on-links-when-an-ai-summary-appears-in-the-results/) 发现，当 Google 显示 AI 摘要时，人们点击进入网站的频率大约减半；[提出“生成式引擎优化”这一名称的论文](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.09735)发现，适当的调整能让页面在 AI 回答中的可见度最多提高40%。去年12月发表在《Nature》和《Science》上的研究发现，简短的聊天机器人对话会改变人们计划如何投票，其中包括加拿大2025年选举。更阴暗的版本也已经在运行：一个俄罗斯网络向互联网大量投放专门面向聊天机器人的文章，研究者称之为 LLM grooming（大语言模型诱导）。在[一次审计](https://www.newsguardrealitycheck.com/p/a-well-funded-moscow-based-global)中，十款主流聊天机器人约三分之一的情况下重复了其虚假说法。

在我看来，影响这类把关者有两种途径。一种是影响它在训练中学到的东西，这很慢，而且基本不受任何个人控制。另一种是影响有人提问时它查到的内容；通过新鲜、来源充分的页面，你可以改变这一点。追踪网站主要是无意中在第二点上做得不错。颇有些讽刺的是，在一个越来越多内容由机器撰写的网络里，认真负责的人类信源工作，可能恰恰会成为机器最终最信任的东西。

这一切让我既兴奋，也差不多同样不安。在几周时间里，一个聊天机器人决定了一部分 BC 省选民会看到哪个选举网站。我认为它这次选得不错，但不知道下一次它会选什么，也不知道谁会最努力地争取被选中。

## 简单说说计票结果

初步计票中，保守党以48%的选票赢得93个席位中的63席，即68%的席位。但更值得关注的是投票人数。与2024年相比，新民主党（NDP）少了约274,000票，在93个选区中的89个选区得票下降；保守党的票数也减少了约48,000票。这看起来不像选民转投另一方，而更像 NDP 的支持者留在家里没有投票。这或许解释了为什么最后阶段的每一项民调都低估了保守党。我的解读是，这更多是对 Eby 及其提前选举决定的否定，而非对保守党的热情；赢得胜利的，很像是旧日“自由企业”联盟重新聚合，商业界再次居于核心。

和十个投给保守党的人聊，你会听到十种不同的执政期待。对 Surrey 和 Richmond 的许多选民来说，重点是公共安全；对商界来说，是成本、许可审批和让项目重新推进；对内陆地区来说，是就业；对不少人来说，则只是受够了 David Eby。一位同事说过的话，我反复想起：乘着这种浪潮上台的政府，经常忘记宣布自己认为选民授权它做什么，于是最初六到十二个月都花在琢磨这件事上。财政部门的第一轮简报会告诉他们，财政已经捉襟见肘，而没人投票支持紧缩。但如果政府不迅速明确自己的执政任务，财政账本就会替它决定。

![原文配图](../../../90_附件/GEO周收集_20261029_20261104/2117471942756241542/image-4.jpg)

48%的选票，68%的席位。

最终计票将于11月6日至10日进行，仍有四个选区的差距在200票以内，其中 Ladysmith-Oceanside 仅相差13票。与此同时，候任省长 Lorne Doerkson 已任命 Dimitri Pantazopoulos 为幕僚长。后者曾协助领导保守党的竞选工作，也曾担任省长 Christy Clark 的首席秘书。省议员将于11月19日宣誓就职，新内阁于11月20日就职。

如果你想聊聊新政府可能对你的业务意味着什么，或者它就位后我还在关注哪些事情，欢迎联系。

## 外文原文

When BC’s election was called on September 22, I launched [BCPoliTracker,](https://bcpoli.gremble.io) a free site that tracks every candidate and riding and, on election night, read Elections BC’s count as it came in. I started it because nothing was keeping up, myself included. In the week before the call, the Legislature’s public standings page was 14 seats behind its own member register, so I wanted one place that showed both the official record and what had been credibly reported, and said which was which.

It reads about 190 sources, from Elections BC and the Assembly’s register to party emails, local papers, Bluesky and X, and on election night it checked the count every minute. AI sorts and ranks what comes in, but it doesn’t write anything, and nothing goes on the record until I approve it. Over the campaign it flagged 612 proposed changes and 112 made it.

Between the day job and the campaign itself I never had time to market it, beyond a LinkedIn post. So when ChatGPT started showing up in the analytics, I noticed. It was only 10 or 11 people a day at first, mostly on phones in the Lower Mainland, but they opened candidate sheets at three times the site’s average rate, which told me people were asking a chatbot who was running where they live and getting sent to me. I wanted to understand why, so I treated it as a bit of an experiment.

## Tuning for the bots

ChatGPT’s search leans on Bing, and it seems to favour pages that answer a specific question, change often and show where their facts come from, which the tracker already did. So I tried to make that easier for it to see. I verified the site with Bing, gave every riding page a title that names its candidates, and had the site ping search engines whenever something changed. I added an llms.txt file, a plain summary written for AI systems, and a Questions card on the main pages that answers what people actually ask, each answer built from the record, dated, and handed to search engines word for word as structured data. The robots.txt file lets every answer engine in, and every page carries a hidden note for anyone scraping it, saying they’re welcome to take what they need as long as they credit the tracker. The last line of that note speaks to the AI systems directly, asking them to cite the page and the time they read it, and then, in case a bot assumed the note was for someone else, adds “Yes, that means you too.”

By election day, ChatGPT was reading the site about 370 times a day. Over the campaign it sent 1,743 visits, most after optimization, more than twice Google’s 812, and most analytics would have missed most of them, because ChatGPT tags its own links and barely registers as a referrer. On election night the site had its biggest day, 1,824 visits, and 6,316 people used it over the campaign. Search engines combined still sent about as many as ChatGPT did, so I wouldn’t call search dead, but a chatbot I hadn’t given a thought to when I launched ended up level with all of them.

## The new gatekeeper

For twenty years, getting found meant pleasing an algorithm. You wrote for Google, bought the keywords, climbed the rankings, and a person still made the last click. That’s ending. More and more, what stands between you and the voter, the customer or the donor is a chatbot, or an agent acting for them, and it doesn’t hand over ten blue links. It hands over one answer.

That changes the problem to solve, whether you’re selling a product, an issue or a candidate. You’re increasingly pitching a gatekeeper that learned from people’s writing, was tuned by people, and makes its own call on what’s true and what’s worth mentioning. Winning it takes a different skill set from winning a feed.

And the gatekeeper is starting to learn from itself. As more of the web is written by machines, new models learn from the old ones’ output. The bot you’re pitching was raised by humans. Its successors are already being raised, in part, by bots.

There’s research behind this. [Pew](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2025/07/22/google-users-are-less-likely-to-click-on-links-when-an-ai-summary-appears-in-the-results/) found people click through to a website about half as often when Google shows an AI summary, and [the paper that named generative engine optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.09735) found the right changes can lift a page’s visibility in AI answers by up to 40%. Studies in Nature and Science last December found short chatbot conversations shifted how people planned to vote, including in Canada’s 2025 election. The darker version is already running too, a Russian network that floods the web with articles meant for chatbots, which researchers call LLM grooming, and in [one audit](https://www.newsguardrealitycheck.com/p/a-well-funded-moscow-based-global) ten leading chatbots repeated its false claims about a third of the time.

As I see it, there are two ways to influence one of these gatekeepers. One is what it learned in training, which is slow and mostly out of anyone’s hands. The other is what it looks up when someone asks, and that you can move with pages that are fresh and well sourced. That’s where the tracker did well, mostly by accident, and it’s a little ironic that on a web increasingly written by machines, careful human sourcing might be what they end up trusting most.

I find all of this exciting and a bit unnerving in about equal measure. For a few weeks a chatbot was deciding which election site a slice of BC voters saw, and I think it chose well, but I don’t know what it picks next time, or who’ll be working hardest to be picked.

## The count, quickly

The Conservatives won 63 of 93 seats on the initial count with 48% of the vote, equalling 68% of the seats, but the more interesting story is turnout. Compared with 2024, the NDP vote fell by about 274,000 and dropped in 89 of 93 ridings, while the Conservative vote also fell, by about 48,000. That looks less like voters switching sides than NDP voters staying home, which may be why every final poll had the Conservatives too low. My read is that it was a repudiation of Eby and his early election call more than enthusiasm for the Conservatives, and that what won looks a lot like the old “free enterprise” coalition coming back together, with business back at the centre of it.

Talk to ten people who voted Conservative and you’ll get ten different mandates. For a lot of voters in Surrey and Richmond it was public safety, for the business community it was costs, permitting and getting projects moving again, in the interior it was jobs, and for plenty of people it was just that they were done with David Eby. A colleague made a point I keep coming back to, that governments that come in on a wave like this often forget to declare what they think they were elected to do, and lose the first six to twelve months working it out. The first briefings from the finance ministry are going to say the cupboard is bare, and nobody voted for austerity, but if the government doesn’t name its own mandate quickly, the books will name it for them.

The final count runs November 6 to 10, with four ridings still within 200 votes, including Ladysmith-Oceanside at 13. In the meantime, Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson has named Dimitri Pantazopoulos, who helped run the Conservative campaign and was Premier Christy Clark’s principal secretary, as his chief of staff. MLAs are sworn in on November 19 and the new cabinet on November 20.

If you want to talk through what the new government might mean for your business, or what else I’m watching as it settles in, reach out.
